Gun Shop Hijack

By: Sasha Schwendenwein | Commission

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
A career conman is now hijacking gun shops. What could go wrong?

Unique Selling Point:
We have undercover footage of him telling us he's expanding his gun business and importing.
We have a police source.
We have amazing informaiton on the conman Jonathan Stephenson from a previous case study.
We did a previous story on Stephenson (Graham did a story on a solar scam in 2021)
We have potential to catch him at a hijacked gun shop.


Summary:
It began with a submission into Carte Blanche.
A firearms dealer, Cobie Englebrecht, wrote in with a warning: two men tried to take over his firearm shop called Gunsafe in Sasolburg – the fronter is a man called Hendrik van Zyl. They arrived as would-be buyers, talking about partnerships and expansion. But Cobie says once they were inside his business, the deal turned dark. They tried to change his CIPC documents to make one of them the director. And the money he was promised? It never arrived. He is being threatened, but luckily he believes he caught on just in time. Others, he says, did not.
One of those dealers, Adri Nel of Marksman Arms, has gone on record in a sworn affidavit. She describes how Van Zyl and his associate wanted to buy their business in Pretoria. Payments for the purchase of the shop never arrived. Next they were told the CIPC directorship changed, and before any more was paid over (R50,000 over 2 years for a R1million) Hendrik was named as director.
They also sold a whole bunch of firearms that had already been sold – people often buy while they’re waiting for their licenses to be approved… many disappeared during this time from the safe…
When access to the premises was later demanded by Hendrik, SAPS were called to intervene. Her statement paints a picture of a firearms dealership being quietly hijacked while the court and police struggled to catch up.
Then a second, more familiar name emerges in the background. In contracts, he is described as an “adviser”. But multiple sources allege he is deeply involved in driving these deals: Johnathan Clive Stephenson — a man previously featured on Carte Blanche in a 2021 investigation into alleged solar scams. Remember him? He essentially apologized in the story, and said he will fix the issues, but never did. Of course that’s not he how he remembers it… He’s told everyone he wronged him, and he was innocent etc.
So I went into the Marksmans Arms undercover, and guess who was on the phone with the manager? Stephenson! I obviously took over the phone conversation and he boasted on the phone about he’s importing firearms “from all over the world – 19 different countries” and opening a gun shop now in Texas too.
Turns out there are other gun stores that say they have had the same problem… Still tracking down those… But I spoke to the police, and they confirmed the investigation and are happy to meet with me and hand over information because… turns out you need a license to be able to sell firearms and that is hard to get! So Stephenson went to court to get that, and told a judge the police were preventing him from operating this store – he and his lawyer neglected to tell the court that there’s a dispute of ownership – but the police said its clear this store was stolen at CIPC.



Further information:
Working Title: Gun Shop Hijack
The tone of this story is “James Bond” look and feel - high-tension thriller, using a cinematic, danger-forward visual language: mystery, reflections and shadow. The presenter will be styled in a tailored suit, we have a police source who will be silhouetted in phone calls. The overall mood is controlled danger: this is about guns and conmen.
We propose to shoot over two and a half days to give the story: One full day will be dedicated to travelling to Sasolburg to interview the case study there and to capture supporting B-roll of the town, the shop exterior and contextual visuals and then also B-roll: including a controlled shooting range for safety-board visuals and presenter links, as well as phone-call silhouettes and dossier-style look.
A second full day will be used to film in Pretoria North with Adri and Dawie Nel, capturing their interviews and presenter links, and then also the previous case study in Joburg South.
Half day for the confront. (VO) Five years ago, we thought we were chasing a dodgy solar scam:
Panels didn’t arrive, and promises evaporated in the sun…

(LINK) [At gun range] We thought that was the end of it… but then the scams multiplied and mutated. The cast of characters grew, and the list of victims exploded. And suddenly, it wasn’t just about solar panels or geysers anymore. But GUNS! [Cocks gun]

(VO) Some things haven’t changed - Jonathan Clive Stephenson is still hiding behind business partners… And it’s not just one gun but entire shops full of them!


(ALBERTO) I started finding more and more people. Fifty, sixty names.
All saying the same thing.

UPSOUND STEPHENSON PHONE I’m bringing weapons in from the States.
We’re opening a gun shop in Texas.

(VO) Why stop at one gun, when you can get the whole store?

(SOURCE) He’s dangerous, wrap sheet as long as my arm.

(LINK) This is the story of how one name keeps reappearing. And why the next chapter could be far more dangerous than the last. [Shoots gun]


(VO) In 2021, Alberto da Silva lost R120,000 to a solar company linked to Stephenson. While a partner fronted the business, he controlled it from the shadows.

Alberto: old story

(VO) Alberto opened a fraud case, but what haunted him most was how, over the next five years, new schemes linked to Stephenson kept popping up and vanishing without him going to jail.

Alberto: (NEW INTV) (At his home in Linmeyer) VO: I was caught cos there was nothing about him online, so I wanted to change that. I started buying the web domains linked to the companies that took my money. I turned them into warning pages. It felt like the only way to stop the next person from getting hurt.

(VO) Alberto says he has now collected the names of more than sixty people who claim they were targeted in similar schemes. He estimates their combined losses run into the millions of rands. The complaints stretch across industries. Outdoor gear. Boreholes. Even church tours.

(LINK) Sources leaked his criminal record which shows more than 40 cases against him. You might think that kind of record would shut doors. Even bar you from owning a firearm. It doesn’t.

(VO) with graphic: Online, Stephenson appears unfazed. Even inviting people on Faceook to come after him (show FB post)

Alberto: He feels untouchable.

(VO) In February, a new submission claimed Stephenson was after his store in Sasolburg. Cobie Englebrecht, says Stephenson and another man, Hendrik van Zyl, approached him to buy his gun dealership - Gun Safe. (https://www.thegunsafe.co.za/)

(COBIE) They started trying to change the directorship before they had paid me. Turns out there was a string of gun stores that had similar complaints…

(VO) We’ve also seen the paper trail of customers who were paying for firearms through a payment plan linked to The Gun Safe. Invoices, proof of payment… but some of those customers say when they went to collect their guns, they were told the firearms were missing.
Visuals: Close-ups of Take 6 Solutions invoices and Capitec payment confirmations.

(VO) Luckily Cobie stopped the transaction… but that wasn’t the case for Adrie and Dawie Nel who owned the Marksmans Arms in Pretoria North.

(Adri) Stephenson and Hendrik approached us to buy the business. They said they would pay fifty thousand rand a month for two years. That’s one million rand in total.

(VO) Marksman Arms was a family business: They build firearms, train people and sell. Dawie spent two decades building it. While it was in his name, Adri ran the operation, and its licences were in her name.

(Adri) The next thing we knew, the directorship had changed. It moved from Dawie to Hendrik. We hadn’t been paid a cent.

(VO) Their lawyers advised them to fight it in court. But that costs money, and eight months later they’d run out of cash. So they also came to us and apparently Carte Blanche is a sore point for Stephenson.

(Adri) He hates you. He says he was innocent.

(VO) That’s not how the camera remembers his apology… (reverse tape noise)

ARCHIVE STEPHENSON: I’m sorry to the people we let down.


(VO) When examining his Modus Operandi it was the same as his previous enterprises: while his name wasn’t on the paperwork, he is named as the deal’s “agent”. We reached out so a source close to police investigation.

See presenter on phone….

Source: He shouldn’t be allowed anywhere near firearms. He doesn’t qualify to own a gun. But he went to court to force police to let him operate a gun shop.
That’s made him enemies. Hendrik has disappeared. We can’t find him. And we believe Stephenson is in the United States trying to source more firearms. A lifestyle audit of Stephenson and his wife Wendy, have over 70 companies together. She is also involved in his cons.

VO: If that doesn’t assure you he’s the boss… then maybe these Whatsapp messages will. The mere “Advisor” reassures buyers that their firearms are “perfectly safe”, blames police delays, and promises he’s buying a new store in Sasolburg…[show whatsapps]

Alberto: A lifestyle audit shows Stephenson and his wife, Wendy, linked to more than seventy companies. His wife is also tied to several of the ventures now under scrutiny.

(VO) In a recorded conversation between Johnathan Clive Stephenson and Adri Nel, about his nonpayment quickly turns aggressive. The audio reveals what many claim, how he asserts control and intimidates those who challenge him.

(Stephenson) That shop there… that’s my shop.

(VO) and that he doesn’t intend to pay for it…

(Stephenson) I will never pay somebody a cent.

(VO) And then come the threats.

(Stephenson) You’re the mother of children. I wanted you to think about that.

(Show Adri’s reaction to listening to recording)

(Stephenson) I make one phone call now… all of you go to jail.

(Adri) He says he has cops on his payroll – he’s very dangerous.

(VO) Adri wasn’t alone. Sworn statements show more verbal abuse and threats when a client asked about firearms that had gone missing. Apparently Stephenson was too busy “fighting SAPS” to deal with him. [show statement]


(LINK) We wanted to test whether the man described on paper as an adviser was still running things behind the scenes. So we sent our producer undercover into the heart of the dispute.

Visual: Producer walks in

(PRODUCER) Okay, I am recording. I’m going into the gun store.

(VO) And then, by pure luck, the alleged adviser just happens to be on the phone. What are the chances. Sometimes journalism gets a little gift.

(STEPHENSON)Hi I’m Jonathan. I’m in America right now. Arizona.

(VO) He tells our producer he’s in the United States for gun shows.

(STEPHENSON) I went to Texas last week for a day because we are opening a shop down there.

(VO) He claims he is in the process of buying a gun shop near Dallas.

(STEPHENSON) We have our own import company now from the States.
We’re the only shop that’s going to have sixteen new guns from the States and Europe.

(VO) A source close to the police investigation tells us firearms have gone missing under his watch.

(POLICE SOURCE) There are reports of guns going missing. At Marksman Arms, firearms registered to customers disappeared.

(VO) It’s not just an allegation between business partners. Customers have invoices. Proof of payment. Approved licences. But some say when they tried to collect their firearms, the guns had vanished.

(VO) With his car no longer outside the shop, we decide it’s time to stop listening. And start asking questions.


(VO) From solar panels… to gun shops. Higher stakes. How does someone accused by so many, in so many cases, still get to travel freely? We put that question to American authorities. And to South African police.

(Adri) Many people bought guns and were waiting for their licenses, those guns have gone missing or have been sold.

(POLICE SOURCE) Many guns went missing…

(LINK) It’s not just an allegation between business partners. Customers have invoices. Proof of payment. Approved licences. But some say when they tried to collect their firearms, the guns had vanished.

Script:


(MacFarlane) Are you afraid for your life? Are you scared?
(Adri Nel) Yes. Yes, I am.
(MacFarlane) In just six months, a family’s world has been turned upside down.
(MacFarlane) A business deal that seemed simple at the time proved to be anything but. Now, out of pocket, they claim to have fallen victim to an abusive scamster.
(Adri) It's quite a shock. I’ve never been in this situation. What do you do?
(MacFarlane) So they, and another of the alleged victims, turned to us. But as we investigated we realised we’d met the alleged scamster before…
His name is Jonathan Stephenson… Once a purveyor of solar panels, now an apparent gun enthusiast.
(MacFarlane) For 13 years, Adri and Dawie Nel ran Marksman Arms — a small firearm dealership in Pretoria serving sport shooters, collectors and - as their home suggests - hunters.
(Adri Nel) It’s quite an intense trust relationship you have to build with people… trusting somebody with your firearm.
(MacFarlane) Last year, the Nels decided to sell their business. They were approached by two men with an offer to purchase: one was this man, Hendrik van Zyl and the other his apparent business partner, Jonathan Stephenson.

(MacFarlane) Who was the person leading this entire deal from the front?
(Adri Nel) Jonathan was leading everything. But Hendrik signed for everything.
(MacFarlane) The contract for just under a million rand was drawn up between Hendrik van Zyl and Adri Nel — despite Adri’s husband, Dawie being the legal owner. The deal was structured around 20 consecutive monthly payments of R50,000. But the payments were never made and, when the Nel’s got lawyers inMacFarlanelved, they received some shocking news.
(Adri) About half an hour later, our lawyer calls us back and says, ‘You have problems. That business is not on your name anymore.’

(MacFarlane) Somehow, without their knowledge, and without a cent being paid, the business was now registered in Hendrik van Zyl’s name.

(Adri) It's unreal, you… like what is happening?

(MacFarlane) But the Nels then signed a second contract, pinning their hopes on van Zyl’s commitment to pay the full purchase price… to no avail.

(MacFarlane) Was there ever any payment made by him to you?
(Adri) There was one payment made from Hendrik.

(MacFarlane) That means a million rand business changed hands for R50,000, with no explanation as to how it had been transferred into Van Zyl’s name in the first place. The Nels’ questions were met with hostility - not from van Zyl, but from his partner, Stephenson.

(Stephenson Subtitle) You’re the mother of children. I wanted you to think about that. I make one phone call now. All of you go to jail.

(MacFarlane) The Nels, though, weren’t suffering alone.

(Eddie) Jonathan was making all the deals and say this, and what he propose, and how he wants to buy the shop.
(MacFarlane) Eddie Groenewald owns this shop called the Gun Safe in Sasolburg, in the Northern Free State. Last year he decided to sell and he was approached by two men… Hendrik Van Zyl and Johnathan Stephenson.
(Eddie) Hi, pleased to meet you.
(Eddie) Everything they said was going onto Hendrik’s name. After about a month, when they came in, we started realizing, but he's not paying.

(MacFarlane) As in the Nels’ case, there was an attempt to change the company’s ownership, despite Van Zyl not having paid the purchase price. Unlike the Nels, Groenewald blocked the move.

(Eddie) They tried to take the responsibility away from me without me knowing it. That's when we start realizing, "Here's the problem."

(MacFarlane) It didn’t take our investigation long to reveal an established MO. Nor did joining the dots around Jonathan Stephenson. Five years ago, we investigated an alleged solar scam after being approached by people who’d paid for panel systems that were never delivered. Alberto da SIlva was one of them, claiming to have lost R90,000.

(Alberto) I've got 67 people that have definitely answered that he’s been scammed to the tune of R3.8 million.

(MacFarlane) And the man alleged to have swindled close to 70 people? Jonathan Stephenson. At the time he denied wrongdoing, attributing his business failure to supplier problems and Covid 19.

The negative publicity appeared to have little, if any, impact. Stephenson — who has faced close to 50 fraud charges — openly taunted the justice system: “I laugh at the South African criminal justice system… Come and get me if you can.”

We understand the police are now investigating Stephenson, and we spoke to an insider close to the case.

(Insider Subtitle) He's not allowed to engage in the gun business.
(MacFarlane) Our insider says that, because he’s facing multiple fraud charges, Stephenson shouldn’t qualify for a firearm licence. He also lacks the competency certification required to handle a gun. That might explain why the gun shop contracts list Hendrik van Zyl as the owner.
(Insider Subtitle) It seems that he's been using people — like in his other scams — to act on his behalf so that he cannot legally be traceable.
(MacFarlane) So how does someone linked to multiple fraud cases apparently end up running a gun shop? Our producer went undercover at the Nels’ gunshop, the Marksman Arms, to try and find out.
As she arrived, an employee was on the phone to Stephenson, who claimed to be in the U.S.

(Employee Subtitle) The boss is on the phone.
(Stephenson Subtitle) I went to Texas last week for a day because we are opening a shop down there.

(MacFarlane) Then, Stephenson announced that he’s importing guns into South Africa.

(Producer Subtitle) So you guys are obviously bringing them in?
(Stephenson Subtitle) Yeah, 16 countries we’re importing them from right now.

(MacFarlane) But importing weapons is strictly regulated and requires very specific licences, raising more questions about Stephenson’s alleged connection to several firearms companies and dealer websites.

And, while Stephenson jets off to the States, it’s claimed Marksman Arms clients are now gunless.

(Adri) Some people got their licences and they went there to collect their firearms… and the firearms wasn't there.
(MacFarlane) Trying to make sense of what our investigation revealed, we call the less outspoken of the two apparent partners, Hendrick van Zyl.
(MacFarlane Subtitle) Are you still inMacFarlanelved in that store?
(Van Zyl Subtitle) No.

(MacFarlane) Van Zyl claims to have resigned from Marksman Arms in January, denying the business hijacking allegations or acting as a front for Stephenson. He claims payments stopped because the business was not properly handed over — an allegation the Nels deny.
But, if he’s no longer the sole director, where does that leave the deal with the Nels?

(Stephenson Subtitle) I work for the gun shop.
(MacFarlane Subtitle) Oh you work for the gun shop?
(Stephenson Subtitle) Yes. And there was no way that the gun shop was taken over illegally.
(MacFarlane) Stephenson denies hijacking the Nels’ store, saying the sale agreement is legitimate. He acknowledges the Nels have only received R50 000 but claims they were the ones who breached the contract.
(Stephenson Subtitle) When we took over the…and did the deal for the shop…
(MacFarlane Subtitle) So you took it over… you didn’t buy it?
(Stephenson Subtitle) No, no, we took over the shop. We were supposed to pay. However, they went to some attorney who cost them an absolute fortune and cost us an absolute fortune.
(MacFarlane) On Groenewald’s shop, The Gun Safe, Stephenson once again shifts blame to the owners.
(Stephenson Subtitle) Plus we have paid them, plus we have delivered over a f***ing million rand of guns to their store that’s still sitting in there still. Indisputable facts.
(MacFarlane) In other words, Stephenson claims he paid the Groenewalds in stock worth a million rand instead of cash. We confirmed that stock was delivered to the shop but, concerned about the attempted hijacking, Groenewald returned it to the supplier. The supplier said Stephenson didn’t pay for the guns.
(MacFarlane Subtitle) Jonathan, you know you've got so many excuses. Are you a career conman?
(Stephenson Subtitle) Who conned them out of their business? We've taken over, we have paid them.
(MacFarlane Subtitle) R50,000 for a million rand business?
(Stephenson Subtitle) They then went to the lawyer…
(MacFarlane Subtitle) Let’s have an interview on camera…
(Stephenson Subtitle) …get all the paperwork and the facts, I want to come to you.


(MacFarlane) But Stephenson didn’t follow through on that offer. Instead he wrote to us denying any wrongdoing. He claims he’s returned stock to all other gun stores but couldn’t do so at the Gun Safe because he was locked out. He says our sources are wrong and that he deals in “facts, bank statements, and contracts.” He denies guns belonging to some of the Nels’ clients weren’t handed to them and, in any event, he says he’s just an employee. News that came as a surprise to Van Zyl.


(Van Zyl Subtitle) No, because he owns those companies. He's the majority shareholder.

(MacFarlane) Through his lawyers, Stephenson says he won’t deal with specific allegations because they’re unsubstantiated.
Groenewald narrowly avoided losing his business. We asked the company registrar how the Marksman Arms ownership changed without the Nels’ knowledge. They say they’re investigating — and the Nels are moving to have it reversed through their lawyers.

Of course that’s not he how he remembers it… He’s told everyone he wronged him, and he was innocent etc. So I went into the Marksmans Arms undercover, and guess who was on the phone with the manager? Stephenson! I obviously took over the phone conversation and he boasted on the phone about he’s importing firearms “from all over the world – 19 different countries” and opening a gun shop now in Texas too. Turns out there are other gun stores that say they have had the same problem… Still tracking down those… But I spoke to the police, and they confirmed the investigation and are happy to meet with me and hand over information because… turns out you need a license to be able to sell firearms and that is hard to get! So Stephenson went to court to get that, and told a judge the police were preventing him from operating this store – he and his lawyer neglected to tell the court that there’s a dispute of ownership – but the police said its clear this store was stolen at CIPC. Further information: Working Title: Gun Shop Hijack The tone of this story is “James Bond” look and feel - high-tension thriller, using a cinematic, danger-forward visual language: mystery, reflections and shadow. The presenter will be styled in a tailored suit, we have a police source who will be silhouetted in phone calls. The overall mood is controlled danger: this is about guns and conmen. We propose to shoot over two and a half days to give the story: One full day will be dedicated to travelling to Sasolburg to interview the case study there and to capture supporting B-roll of the town, the shop exterior and contextual visuals and then also B-roll: including a controlled shooting range for safety-board visuals and presenter links, as well as phone-call silhouettes and dossier-style look. A second full day will be used to film in Pretoria North with Adri and Dawie Nel, capturing their interviews and presenter links, and then also the previous case study in Joburg South. Half day for the confront. (VO) Five years ago, we thought we were chasing a dodgy solar scam: Panels didn’t arrive, and promises evaporated in the sun… (LINK) [At gun range] We thought that was the end of it… but then the scams multiplied and mutated. The cast of characters grew, and the list of victims exploded. And suddenly, it wasn’t just about solar panels or geysers anymore. But GUNS! [Cocks gun] (VO) Some things haven’t changed - Jonathan Clive Stephenson is still hiding behind business partners… And it’s not just one gun but entire shops full of them! (ALBERTO) I started finding more and more people. Fifty, sixty names. All saying the same thing. UPSOUND STEPHENSON PHONE I’m bringing weapons in from the States. We’re opening a gun shop in Texas. (VO) Why stop at one gun, when you can get the whole store? (SOURCE) He’s dangerous, wrap sheet as long as my arm. (LINK) This is the story of how one name keeps reappearing. And why the next chapter could be far more dangerous than the last. [Shoots gun] (VO) In 2021, Alberto da Silva lost R120,000 to a solar company linked to Stephenson. While a partner fronted the business, he controlled it from the shadows. Alberto: old story (VO) Alberto opened a fraud case, but what haunted him most was how, over the next five years, new schemes linked to Stephenson kept popping up and vanishing without him going to jail. Alberto: (NEW INTV) (At his home in Linmeyer) VO: I was caught cos there was nothing about him online, so I wanted to change that. I started buying the web domains linked to the companies that took my money. I turned them into warning pages. It felt like the only way to stop the next person from getting hurt. (VO) Alberto says he has now collected the names of more than sixty people who claim they were targeted in similar schemes. He estimates their combined losses run into the millions of rands. The complaints stretch across industries. Outdoor gear. Boreholes. Even church tours. (LINK) Sources leaked his criminal record which shows more than 40 cases against him. You might think that kind of record would shut doors. Even bar you from owning a firearm. It doesn’t. (VO) with graphic: Online, Stephenson appears unfazed. Even inviting people on Faceook to come after him (show FB post) Alberto: He feels untouchable. (VO) In February, a new submission claimed Stephenson was after his store in Sasolburg. Cobie Englebrecht, says Stephenson and another man, Hendrik van Zyl, approached him to buy his gun dealership - Gun Safe. (https://www.thegunsafe.co.za/) (COBIE) They started trying to change the directorship before they had paid me. Turns out there was a string of gun stores that had similar complaints… (VO) We’ve also seen the paper trail of customers who were paying for firearms through a payment plan linked to The Gun Safe. Invoices, proof of payment… but some of those customers say when they went to collect their guns, they were told the firearms were missing. Visuals: Close-ups of Take 6 Solutions invoices and Capitec payment confirmations. (VO) Luckily Cobie stopped the transaction… but that wasn’t the case for Adrie and Dawie Nel who owned the Marksmans Arms in Pretoria North. (Adri) Stephenson and Hendrik approached us to buy the business. They said they would pay fifty thousand rand a month for two years. That’s one million rand in total. (VO) Marksman Arms was a family business: They build firearms, train people and sell. Dawie spent two decades building it. While it was in his name, Adri ran the operation, and its licences were in her name. (Adri) The next thing we knew, the directorship had changed. It moved from Dawie to Hendrik. We hadn’t been paid a cent. (VO) Their lawyers advised them to fight it in court. But that costs money, and eight months later they’d run out of cash. So they also came to us and apparently Carte Blanche is a sore point for Stephenson. (Adri) He hates you. He says he was innocent. (VO) That’s not how the camera remembers his apology… (reverse tape noise) ARCHIVE STEPHENSON: I’m sorry to the people we let down. (VO) When examining his Modus Operandi it was the same as his previous enterprises: while his name wasn’t on the paperwork, he is named as the deal’s “agent”. We reached out so a source close to police investigation. See presenter on phone…. Source: He shouldn’t be allowed anywhere near firearms. He doesn’t qualify to own a gun. But he went to court to force police to let him operate a gun shop. That’s made him enemies. Hendrik has disappeared. We can’t find him. And we believe Stephenson is in the United States trying to source more firearms. A lifestyle audit of Stephenson and his wife Wendy, have over 70 companies together. She is also involved in his cons. VO: If that doesn’t assure you he’s the boss… then maybe these Whatsapp messages will. The mere “Advisor” reassures buyers that their firearms are “perfectly safe”, blames police delays, and promises he’s buying a new store in Sasolburg…[show whatsapps] Alberto: A lifestyle audit shows Stephenson and his wife, Wendy, linked to more than seventy companies. His wife is also tied to several of the ventures now under scrutiny. (VO) In a recorded conversation between Johnathan Clive Stephenson and Adri Nel, about his nonpayment quickly turns aggressive. The audio reveals what many claim, how he asserts control and intimidates those who challenge him. (Stephenson) That shop there… that’s my shop. (VO) and that he doesn’t intend to pay for it… (Stephenson) I will never pay somebody a cent. (VO) And then come the threats. (Stephenson) You’re the mother of children. I wanted you to think about that. (Show Adri’s reaction to listening to recording) (Stephenson) I make one phone call now… all of you go to jail. (Adri) He says he has cops on his payroll – he’s very dangerous. (VO) Adri wasn’t alone. Sworn statements show more verbal abuse and threats when a client asked about firearms that had gone missing. Apparently Stephenson was too busy “fighting SAPS” to deal with him. [show statement] (LINK) We wanted to test whether the man described on paper as an adviser was still running things behind the scenes. So we sent our producer undercover into the heart of the dispute. Visual: Producer walks in (PRODUCER) Okay, I am recording. I’m going into the gun store. (VO) And then, by pure luck, the alleged adviser just happens to be on the phone. What are the chances. Sometimes journalism gets a little gift. (STEPHENSON)Hi I’m Jonathan. I’m in America right now. Arizona. (VO) He tells our producer he’s in the United States for gun shows. (STEPHENSON) I went to Texas last week for a day because we are opening a shop down there. (VO) He claims he is in the process of buying a gun shop near Dallas. (STEPHENSON) We have our own import company now from the States. We’re the only shop that’s going to have sixteen new guns from the States and Europe. (VO) A source close to the police investigation tells us firearms have gone missing under his watch. (POLICE SOURCE) There are reports of guns going missing. At Marksman Arms, firearms registered to customers disappeared. (VO) It’s not just an allegation between business partners. Customers have invoices. Proof of payment. Approved licences. But some say when they tried to collect their firearms, the guns had vanished. (VO) With his car no longer outside the shop, we decide it’s time to stop listening. And start asking questions. (VO) From solar panels… to gun shops. Higher stakes. How does someone accused by so many, in so many cases, still get to travel freely? We put that question to American authorities. And to South African police. (Adri) Many people bought guns and were waiting for their licenses, those guns have gone missing or have been sold. (POLICE SOURCE) Many guns went missing… (LINK) It’s not just an allegation between business partners. Customers have invoices. Proof of payment. Approved licences. But some say when they tried to collect their firearms, the guns had vanished. Script: (MacFarlane) Are you afraid for your life? Are you scared? (Adri Nel) Yes. Yes, I am. (MacFarlane) In just six months, a family’s world has been turned upside down. (MacFarlane) A business deal that seemed simple at the time proved to be anything but. Now, out of pocket, they claim to have fallen victim to an abusive scamster. (Adri) It's quite a shock. I’ve never been in this situation. What do you do? (MacFarlane) So they, and another of the alleged victims, turned to us. But as we investigated we realised we’d met the alleged scamster before… His name is Jonathan Stephenson… Once a purveyor of solar panels, now an apparent gun enthusiast. (MacFarlane) For 13 years, Adri and Dawie Nel ran Marksman Arms — a small firearm dealership in Pretoria serving sport shooters, collectors and - as their home suggests - hunters. (Adri Nel) It’s quite an intense trust relationship you have to build with people… trusting somebody with your firearm. (MacFarlane) Last year, the Nels decided to sell their business. They were approached by two men with an offer to purchase: one was this man, Hendrik van Zyl and the other his apparent business partner, Jonathan Stephenson. (MacFarlane) Who was the person leading this entire deal from the front? (Adri Nel) Jonathan was leading everything. But Hendrik signed for everything. (MacFarlane) The contract for just under a million rand was drawn up between Hendrik van Zyl and Adri Nel — despite Adri’s husband, Dawie being the legal owner. The deal was structured around 20 consecutive monthly payments of R50,000. But the payments were never made and, when the Nel’s got lawyers inMacFarlanelved, they received some shocking news. (Adri) About half an hour later, our lawyer calls us back and says, ‘You have problems. That business is not on your name anymore.’ (MacFarlane) Somehow, without their knowledge, and without a cent being paid, the business was now registered in Hendrik van Zyl’s name. (Adri) It's unreal, you… like what is happening? (MacFarlane) But the Nels then signed a second contract, pinning their hopes on van Zyl’s commitment to pay the full purchase price… to no avail. (MacFarlane) Was there ever any payment made by him to you? (Adri) There was one payment made from Hendrik. (MacFarlane) That means a million rand business changed hands for R50,000, with no explanation as to how it had been transferred into Van Zyl’s name in the first place. The Nels’ questions were met with hostility - not from van Zyl, but from his partner, Stephenson. (Stephenson Subtitle) You’re the mother of children. I wanted you to think about that. I make one phone call now. All of you go to jail. (MacFarlane) The Nels, though, weren’t suffering alone. (Eddie) Jonathan was making all the deals and say this, and what he propose, and how he wants to buy the shop. (MacFarlane) Eddie Groenewald owns this shop called the Gun Safe in Sasolburg, in the Northern Free State. Last year he decided to sell and he was approached by two men… Hendrik Van Zyl and Johnathan Stephenson. (Eddie) Hi, pleased to meet you. (Eddie) Everything they said was going onto Hendrik’s name. After about a month, when they came in, we started realizing, but he's not paying. (MacFarlane) As in the Nels’ case, there was an attempt to change the company’s ownership, despite Van Zyl not having paid the purchase price. Unlike the Nels, Groenewald blocked the move. (Eddie) They tried to take the responsibility away from me without me knowing it. That's when we start realizing, "Here's the problem." (MacFarlane) It didn’t take our investigation long to reveal an established MO. Nor did joining the dots around Jonathan Stephenson. Five years ago, we investigated an alleged solar scam after being approached by people who’d paid for panel systems that were never delivered. Alberto da SIlva was one of them, claiming to have lost R90,000. (Alberto) I've got 67 people that have definitely answered that he’s been scammed to the tune of R3.8 million. (MacFarlane) And the man alleged to have swindled close to 70 people? Jonathan Stephenson. At the time he denied wrongdoing, attributing his business failure to supplier problems and Covid 19. The negative publicity appeared to have little, if any, impact. Stephenson — who has faced close to 50 fraud charges — openly taunted the justice system: “I laugh at the South African criminal justice system… Come and get me if you can.” We understand the police are now investigating Stephenson, and we spoke to an insider close to the case. (Insider Subtitle) He's not allowed to engage in the gun business. (MacFarlane) Our insider says that, because he’s facing multiple fraud charges, Stephenson shouldn’t qualify for a firearm licence. He also lacks the competency certification required to handle a gun. That might explain why the gun shop contracts list Hendrik van Zyl as the owner. (Insider Subtitle) It seems that he's been using people — like in his other scams — to act on his behalf so that he cannot legally be traceable. (MacFarlane) So how does someone linked to multiple fraud cases apparently end up running a gun shop? Our producer went undercover at the Nels’ gunshop, the Marksman Arms, to try and find out. As she arrived, an employee was on the phone to Stephenson, who claimed to be in the U.S. (Employee Subtitle) The boss is on the phone. (Stephenson Subtitle) I went to Texas last week for a day because we are opening a shop down there. (MacFarlane) Then, Stephenson announced that he’s importing guns into South Africa. (Producer Subtitle) So you guys are obviously bringing them in? (Stephenson Subtitle) Yeah, 16 countries we’re importing them from right now. (MacFarlane) But importing weapons is strictly regulated and requires very specific licences, raising more questions about Stephenson’s alleged connection to several firearms companies and dealer websites. And, while Stephenson jets off to the States, it’s claimed Marksman Arms clients are now gunless. (Adri) Some people got their licences and they went there to collect their firearms… and the firearms wasn't there. (MacFarlane) Trying to make sense of what our investigation revealed, we call the less outspoken of the two apparent partners, Hendrick van Zyl. (MacFarlane Subtitle) Are you still inMacFarlanelved in that store? (Van Zyl Subtitle) No. (MacFarlane) Van Zyl claims to have resigned from Marksman Arms in January, denying the business hijacking allegations or acting as a front for Stephenson. He claims payments stopped because the business was not properly handed over — an allegation the Nels deny. But, if he’s no longer the sole director, where does that leave the deal with the Nels? (Stephenson Subtitle) I work for the gun shop. (MacFarlane Subtitle) Oh you work for the gun shop? (Stephenson Subtitle) Yes. And there was no way that the gun shop was taken over illegally. (MacFarlane) Stephenson denies hijacking the Nels’ store, saying the sale agreement is legitimate. He acknowledges the Nels have only received R50 000 but claims they were the ones who breached the contract. (Stephenson Subtitle) When we took over the…and did the deal for the shop… (MacFarlane Subtitle) So you took it over… you didn’t buy it? (Stephenson Subtitle) No, no, we took over the shop. We were supposed to pay. However, they went to some attorney who cost them an absolute fortune and cost us an absolute fortune. (MacFarlane) On Groenewald’s shop, The Gun Safe, Stephenson once again shifts blame to the owners. (Stephenson Subtitle) Plus we have paid them, plus we have delivered over a f***ing million rand of guns to their store that’s still sitting in there still. Indisputable facts. (MacFarlane) In other words, Stephenson claims he paid the Groenewalds in stock worth a million rand instead of cash. We confirmed that stock was delivered to the shop but, concerned about the attempted hijacking, Groenewald returned it to the supplier. The supplier said Stephenson didn’t pay for the guns. (MacFarlane Subtitle) Jonathan, you know you've got so many excuses. Are you a career conman? (Stephenson Subtitle) Who conned them out of their business? We've taken over, we have paid them. (MacFarlane Subtitle) R50,000 for a million rand business? (Stephenson Subtitle) They then went to the lawyer… (MacFarlane Subtitle) Let’s have an interview on camera… (Stephenson Subtitle) …get all the paperwork and the facts, I want to come to you. (MacFarlane) But Stephenson didn’t follow through on that offer. Instead he wrote to us denying any wrongdoing. He claims he’s returned stock to all other gun stores but couldn’t do so at the Gun Safe because he was locked out. He says our sources are wrong and that he deals in “facts, bank statements, and contracts.” He denies guns belonging to some of the Nels’ clients weren’t handed to them and, in any event, he says he’s just an employee. News that came as a surprise to Van Zyl. (Van Zyl Subtitle) No, because he owns those companies. He's the majority shareholder. (MacFarlane) Through his lawyers, Stephenson says he won’t deal with specific allegations because they’re unsubstantiated. Groenewald narrowly avoided losing his business. We asked the company registrar how the Marksman Arms ownership changed without the Nels’ knowledge. They say they’re investigating — and the Nels are moving to have it reversed through their lawyers.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): A career conman is now hijacking gun shops. What could go wrong?
metadata.Unique Selling Point: We have undercover footage of him telling us he's expanding his gun business and importing. We have a police source. We have amazing informaiton on the conman Jonathan Stephenson from a previous case study. We did a previous story on Stephenson (Graham did a story on a solar scam in 2021) We have potential to catch him at a hijacked gun shop.
metadata.Summary: It began with a submission into Carte Blanche. A firearms dealer, Cobie Englebrecht, wrote in with a warning: two men tried to take over his firearm shop called Gunsafe in Sasolburg – the fronter is a man called Hendrik van Zyl. They arrived as would-be buyers, talking about partnerships and expansion. But Cobie says once they were inside his business, the deal turned dark. They tried to change his CIPC documents to make one of them the director. And the money he was promised? It never arrived. He is being threatened, but luckily he believes he caught on just in time. Others, he says, did not. One of those dealers, Adri Nel of Marksman Arms, has gone on record in a sworn affidavit. She describes how Van Zyl and his associate wanted to buy their business in Pretoria. Payments for the purchase of the shop never arrived. Next they were told the CIPC directorship changed, and before any more was paid over (R50,000 over 2 years for a R1million) Hendrik was named as director. They also sold a whole bunch of firearms that had already been sold – people often buy while they’re waiting for their licenses to be approved… many disappeared during this time from the safe… When access to the premises was later demanded by Hendrik, SAPS were called to intervene. Her statement paints a picture of a firearms dealership being quietly hijacked while the court and police struggled to catch up. Then a second, more familiar name emerges in the background. In contracts, he is described as an “adviser”. But multiple sources allege he is deeply involved in driving these deals: Johnathan Clive Stephenson — a man previously featured on Carte Blanche in a 2021 investigation into alleged solar scams. Remember him? He essentially apologized in the story, and said he will fix the issues, but never did. Of course that’s not he how he remembers it… He’s told everyone he wronged him, and he was innocent etc. So I went into the Marksmans Arms undercover, and guess who was on the phone with the manager? Stephenson! I obviously took over the phone conversation and he boasted on the phone about he’s importing firearms “from all over the world – 19 different countries” and opening a gun shop now in Texas too. Turns out there are other gun stores that say they have had the same problem… Still tracking down those… But I spoke to the police, and they confirmed the investigation and are happy to meet with me and hand over information because… turns out you need a license to be able to sell firearms and that is hard to get! So Stephenson went to court to get that, and told a judge the police were preventing him from operating this store – he and his lawyer neglected to tell the court that there’s a dispute of ownership – but the police said its clear this store was stolen at CIPC.

Cobie Englebrecht, says Stephenson and another man, Hendrik van Zyl, approached him to buy his gun dealership - Gun Safe. (https://www.thegunsafe.co.za/) (COBIE) They started trying to change the directorship before they had paid me. Turns out there was a string of gun stores that had similar complaints… (VO) We’ve also seen the paper trail of customers who were paying for firearms through a payment plan linked to The Gun Safe. Invoices, proof of payment… but some of those customers say when they went to collect their guns, they were told the firearms were missing. Visuals: Close-ups of Take 6 Solutions invoices and Capitec payment confirmations. (VO) Luckily Cobie stopped the transaction… but that wasn’t the case for Adrie and Dawie Nel who owned the Marksmans Arms in Pretoria North. (Adri) Stephenson and Hendrik approached us to buy the business. They said they would pay fifty thousand rand a month for two years. That’s one million rand in total. (VO) Marksman Arms was a family business: They build firearms, train people and sell. Dawie spent two decades building it. While it was in his name, Adri ran the operation, and its licences were in her name. (Adri) The next thing we knew, the directorship had changed. It moved from Dawie to Hendrik. We hadn’t been paid a cent. (VO) Their lawyers advised them to fight it in court. But that costs money, and eight months later they’d run out of cash. So they also came to us and apparently Carte Blanche is a sore point for Stephenson. (Adri) He hates you. He says he was innocent. (VO) That’s not how the camera remembers his apology… (reverse tape noise) ARCHIVE STEPHENSON: I’m sorry to the people we let down. (VO) When examining his Modus Operandi it was the same as his previous enterprises: while his name wasn’t on the paperwork, he is named as the deal’s “agent”. We reached out so a source close to police investigation. See presenter on phone…. Source: He shouldn’t be allowed anywhere near firearms. He doesn’t qualify to own a gun. But he went to court to force police to let him operate a gun shop. That’s made him enemies. Hendrik has disappeared. We can’t find him. And we believe Stephenson is in the United States trying to source more firearms. A lifestyle audit of Stephenson and his wife Wendy, have over 70 companies together. She is also involved in his cons. VO: If that doesn’t assure you he’s the boss… then maybe these Whatsapp messages will. The mere “Advisor” reassures buyers that their firearms are “perfectly safe”, blames police delays, and promises he’s buying a new store in Sasolburg…[show whatsapps] Alberto: A lifestyle audit shows Stephenson and his wife, Wendy, linked to more than seventy companies. His wife is also tied to several of the ventures now under scrutiny. (VO) In a recorded conversation between Johnathan Clive Stephenson and Adri Nel, about his nonpayment quickly turns aggressive. The audio reveals what many claim, how he asserts control and intimidates those who challenge him. (Stephenson) That shop there… that’s my shop. (VO) and that he doesn’t intend to pay for it… (Stephenson) I will never pay somebody a cent. (VO) And then come the threats. (Stephenson) You’re the mother of children. I wanted you to think about that. (Show Adri’s reaction to listening to recording) (Stephenson) I make one phone call now… all of you go to jail. (Adri) He says he has cops on his payroll – he’s very dangerous. (VO) Adri wasn’t alone. Sworn statements show more verbal abuse and threats when a client asked about firearms that had gone missing. Apparently Stephenson was too busy “fighting SAPS” to deal with him. [show statement] (LINK) We wanted to test whether the man described on paper as an adviser was still running things behind the scenes. So we sent our producer undercover into the heart of the dispute. Visual: Producer walks in (PRODUCER) Okay, I am recording. I’m going into the gun store. (VO) And then, by pure luck, the alleged adviser just happens to be on the phone. What are the chances. Sometimes journalism gets a little gift. (STEPHENSON)Hi I’m Jonathan. I’m in America right now. Arizona. (VO) He tells our producer he’s in the United States for gun shows. (STEPHENSON) I went to Texas last week for a day because we are opening a shop down there. We’re the only shop that’s going to have sixteen new guns from the States and Europe. (VO) A source close to the police investigation tells us firearms have gone missing under his watch.
